I Am a Single Mother to a Teenage Son. How Do I Talk to My Teenage Son About Healthy Relationships? What Should My Son Know About Social Media and Dating?
Tanisha RaoUpdated : May 18, 2026, 11:08 IST
How Do I Talk to My Teenage Son About Social Media and Dating?


These conversations can feel intimidating, especially because it is hard to know where to begin or how much to say. The good news is that it does not have to be one big, serious talk. In fact, it usually works better as an ongoing conversation that evolves over time, where your son feels safe asking questions and sharing his thoughts without fear of being judged or shut down.

Avoid starting from where you think the right place is, as that may result in a conversation that feels awkward, forced or clunky, and your son may feel uncomfortable and try to tune you out. Instead, find a way to understand what he already knows or what he currently wonders about the world of sex and relationships, and establish yourself as a calm and non-judgemental adult who he can turn to for helpful advice rather than turn to friends with no life experience or strangers online who may not offer the right advice for him.

When it comes to relationships, what matters most is helping him understand respect, consent, emotional responsibility, and communication. This includes recognising boundaries, handling rejection, and understanding that relationships are not just about attraction but also about how you treat another person. With social media, it becomes important to talk about how online spaces can distort expectations around bodies, relationships, and attention, and how validation through likes or messages does not always reflect real connection. He also needs to be able to think deeply about safety on digital spaces both for himself and for the people he speaks with, and this requires you to be up-to-date on how younger generations use the internet to socialise and build deep connections too. Do not be afraid to reach out to therapists, adolescent behavioural specialists and sex educators who may be able to guide you on what to expect when it comes to teenagers and their rapidly evolving relationships with the internet.

You do not need to have perfect answers. Being open, honest, and willing to listen goes a long way. It can also help to share your own values and perspectives in a way that feels relatable rather than instructional, so that the conversation feels like guidance rather than a lecture. Do not be embarrassed to admit when you do not have an answer to something, and reassure him that you would like to look into his area of concern and come back to him once you find an answer. What he needs is a safe adult who gives him room to explore himself, have new experiences, be confused with, be scared with, receive helpful advice and validation from, while also being able to make mistakes and develop an instinct for taking accountability and repairing from any harm he may cause. What you are building is trust, so that he knows he can come to you as he navigates these experiences. But it is so much more. It is an environment that fosters his individuality and humanity, where he can be both vulnerable and responsible, and these conversations will form the foundation for how he sees the world and himself for years to come.

You may make mistakes of your own, and it is important to take responsibility and commit to repairing the space when you do, as your son is not only learning from your advice but learning by emulating you too. Let him see that mistakes are normal, and that growing into an adult is not about perfection without mistakes but about repairing and learning with grace.
